subject: Climate & Environment
title: How Acid Rain Forms
description: A micro-lesson that makes How Acid Rain Forms usable.

hook.text: In the 1970s, lakes in Scandinavia started dying. Fish vanished. Forests turned brown.

buildup.text: The cause: SO₂ and NO₂ from British and German coal plants drifting north on the wind.

discovery.text: These gases mix with water vapor to form sulfuric and nitric acid — then fall as rain.

twist.text: Acid rain doesn't burn skin. It works slowly, leaching minerals from soil over years.

climax.text: Regulation cut SO₂ by 90% in Europe and North America. Acid rain is now mostly history there.

punchline.text: Acid rain was solved by laws, not luck.

quiz.question: What causes acid rain?
options: SO₂ and NO₂ mixing with water vapor

details.summary: Acid rain forms when sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides emitted by power plants and vehicles react with water and oxygen in the atmosphere to produce sulfuric and nitric acids. These acids fall as rain, snow, or dry particles, damaging ecosystems and structures.
details.whyItMatters: Acid rain devastated lakes and forests across North America and Europe before emissions cuts proved it could be reversed. It remains a cautionary success story for pollution policy.
takeaways: SO2 and NOx transform into sulfuric and nitric acid in clouds
Acid rain lowers lake pH, killing fish and aquatic insects
US and European SO2 caps reversed acid rain damage within decades

faq.question: Can acid rain damage buildings and monuments?
faq.answer: Yes. Sulfuric and nitric acids dissolve calcium carbonate in limestone and marble, eroding statues, facades, and historical monuments. The Parthenon and many European cathedrals show centuries of acid rain damage.

faq.question: Has acid rain been solved in North America?
faq.answer: SO2 emissions have dropped over 90 percent since the 1990 Clean Air Act amendments, and many lakes and forests are recovering. However, some soils remain depleted of calcium, and nitrogen deposition continues in some areas.
